# Forensic Dossier — Webuild S.p.A. (Milan: WBD)

**Date:** 2026-07-16 · **Price used:** €2.162 (Borsa Italiana, MIL, close 2026-07-16) · **Market value:** €2.13bn on ~987m shares
**Sector:** Industrials (heavy civil engineering & construction) · **Screener tag:** deep value

### A note on the evidence base

No earnings-call transcript was bundled with this name, and the paid data feed carries neither a transcript history nor a news history for this listing. I checked. So this dossier is not built on eight quarters of management dialogue — it is built on the primary documents and the dated public record: the full-year 2025 results release of 12 March 2026, the results call as reported by MarketScreener and FIRSTonline that day, the NEOM contract-termination release of 21 May 2026, the first-quarter order update of May 2026, and the audited balance-sheet and cash-flow data. Where I quote management, I quote what a named outlet reported them saying, and I say so. I have not invented a single figure or phrase.

One housekeeping point that matters, because the ticker is a trap: **WBD on Borsa Italiana is Webuild, the Italian infrastructure contractor formerly called Salini Impregilo. It is not Warner Bros. Discovery**, which trades under the same three letters in the United States and appears elsewhere in our regime notes. Everything below concerns the Italian builder, in euros.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story Webuild told for three years was a growth story, and on its own terms the company delivered it. The 2023–2025 business plan, branded "Roadmap to 2025 – The Future is Now," promised roughly 10% annual revenue growth. Webuild produced a 19% compound rate instead: revenue rose 68% from 2022 to a record €13.6bn in 2025, and operating profit before depreciation (EBITDA — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a rough proxy for cash operating profit) doubled over the same span, with the margin climbing from 7.2% to 8.6%. That is genuine over-delivery against a publicly stated target, and it deserves to be said plainly before anything critical follows.

The arc breaks on 12 March 2026. That is the day the plan ended and the company had to say what comes next — and it declined to. Chief executive Pietro Salini told the results call that the economic environment was too uncertain for specific 2026 targets, and that setting detailed forecasts under such conditions "would not be appropriate" (as reported by MarketScreener and FIRSTonline, 12 March 2026). Revenue for 2026 was described only as being in line with 2025's record. A company that had just beaten every number in its plan chose the moment of maximum credibility to stop giving numbers. The market read that as it reads such things: the shares fell almost 10% that day, to around €2.68, and have not recovered.

The second shift in the arc is geographic, and it was forced rather than chosen. Through 2025 the narrative carried Saudi Arabia's NEOM gigaproject as a growth pillar. In 2026 that pillar was removed by the client, not by the strategist: NEOM terminated the three-dam contract in March 2026 (€2.8bn of backlog) and then the Connector High-Speed Line on 21 May 2026, effective 27 May, at roughly 20% completion. Webuild's own release states that "with this termination, all of Webuild's activities for NEOM have been concluded." The story has since been re-labelled — the May order update emphasised that new work is "in low-risk markets such as Italy, Australia and North America — fully in line with the group's de-risking strategy." De-risking is the right strategy. But it is being narrated as a choice after the client made the choice for them, and that is a tell worth recording.

What was quietly dropped: specific forward guidance. What was quietly introduced: the language of caution, discipline and de-risking, in a company that spent three years talking about scale.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

This is where the dossier earns its keep. Webuild's headline claims about profit are true. Its headline claim about cash is a definitional artifact, and underneath it the cash trajectory is the worst in four years.

| Management's claim | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Record revenue €13.6bn, +15% | Confirmed. The data feed's revenue line reads €12.64bn; the gap is the company including other/joint-venture income in its headline. Direction and magnitude hold. | **Matches** |
| EBITDA €1.16bn, +18%; margin up to 8.6% from 7.2% in 2022 | Confirmed and genuinely good. Margin expansion is real. | **Matches** |
| Adjusted net profit €280m, +13% | Reported net profit €239.8m; earnings per share €0.24 on 984m diluted shares. Both figures are records. | **Matches** |
| "Positive net cash on a standard basis of €772m, beyond guidance" | **This is the problem.** The audited balance sheet at 31 Dec 2025 shows gross borrowings of €3.07bn against cash of €2.44bn — i.e. **net debt of €623m** including €95m of leases (€528m excluding them). The company's €772m "net cash" is a house definition that adds back roughly €1.4bn of financial assets and receivables. It is a disclosed convention, not a fabrication — but it is the opposite sign to the balance sheet. | **Diverges — materially** |
| Backlog €58.4bn "guarantees wide visibility" | Confirmed at year-end, but ~€3.8bn of NEOM work has since been terminated. The May 2026 release concedes construction backlog is now "above €50 billion." | **Matches, then eroded by events** |

The claims above are about profit. Here is what happened to cash, which nobody put in a headline:

| Year | Operating cash flow | Capital spend | **Free cash flow** | Year-end cash | True net debt (incl. leases) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | €1,893m | €441m | **+€1,452m** | €3,061m | €452m net **cash** |
| 2024 | €1,116m | €825m | **+€291m** | €3,215m | €270m net **cash** |
| 2025 | €312m | €869m | **−€557m** | €2,445m | **€623m net debt** |

Three facts follow, and they are the heart of this name:

1. **Free cash flow has fallen for three straight years and is now sharply negative** — from +€1.45bn to −€557m — in the same three years that revenue rose 36% and profit rose 93%. Cash operating flow collapsed by 83% in one year while EBITDA rose 18%.
2. **The cash balance fell €770m in 2025** and true net debt swung by roughly €893m, from net cash to net debt — in the year the company announced net cash "beyond guidance."
3. **Shareholders' equity actually declined**, from €1,713m to €1,675m, despite €240m of record profit. Book value per share has compounded at 0.0% over five years. A company earning record profits whose book value does not grow is not, in the economic sense, earning.

The reconciliation is not mysterious, and it is not fraud. Capital spending of €869m ran at 6.9% of revenue and well above the €487m depreciation charge — the business consumes more capital than it wears out. Working capital drained a further €596m. Net financial charges of €410m and an effective tax rate of 49.6% then take most of what EBITDA produces: €1.16bn of EBITDA becomes €673m of operating profit, €382m of pre-tax profit, and €240m at the bottom. EBITDA, for this company, is not a proxy for owner earnings. It is roughly four times them.

One claim I will not hold against them: the screener flags gross margin "contracting" to 22.8%. That is largely a reclassification in the data feed — administrative costs that sat in one line in 2024 moved to another in 2025. The company's own EBITDA margin *expanded*. I am not going to indict management on an accounting mapping artifact.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining** — and the decline is datable to a single day.

Through the plan period the tone was expansive and target-anchored: management set a 10% growth goal publicly and beat it by nine points, and said so. Confidence was expressed in the way that actually counts — in numbers they could be held to.

On 12 March 2026 that changed. Declining to set 2026 targets because forecasts "would not be appropriate" is defensive language, and it is the most specific piece of evidence in this file. Analysts on the call, as reported that day, described the outlook as "vague" and pressed on Middle East exposure. The shares fell ~10%. Two weeks later, on 26 March 2026, Equita cut its target price to €3.50 from €4.10 explicitly citing greater Middle East business risk — the analysts' worry, priced.

By May the tone had shifted again, to reassurance: new orders concentrated in "low-risk markets," Middle East exposure characterised as only ~5% of backlog, 2026 revenue guidance reaffirmed at 2025 levels. This is the classic movement from offence (scale, growth, plan) to defence (discipline, de-risking, low-risk markets). Nothing in it is dishonest. All of it is defensive.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium — an unusual split verdict, and the split is the finding.**

On operational guidance, Webuild's record is genuinely strong. The 2023–2025 plan targeted ~10% revenue growth and delivered 19%. Margin targets were beaten. This is a management team that hit what it said it would hit, over three years, in a hard industry. Credit where due.

On the balance sheet, the guidance is where the credibility leaks. Management guided to, and then celebrated beating, a "net cash" figure of €772m on a definition that reports the opposite sign to the audited balance sheet's €623m of net debt. The measure is disclosed and consistently applied, so this is presentation, not deception. But it is presentation that flatters in exactly the dimension where the business is weakest, in exactly the year that dimension deteriorated by €893m. When a company chooses to headline a bespoke metric precisely where the standard metric turned against it, a director should mark the disclosure down, not the arithmetic.

And the forward-looking credibility has now been voluntarily surrendered. There is no 2026 earnings target to hold them to, by their own choice. You cannot beat guidance you did not give, and you cannot be scored on it either. That is a reliability question the next plan will have to answer.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Two pressure points are on the record, and both later turned into news.

**Middle East exposure.** Analysts pushed on it during the 12 March call; management characterised it as limited. Ten weeks later NEOM had terminated everything. The analysts were right to push; the €2.8bn dam termination in March and the Connector termination on 21 May settled the argument. In fairness to Webuild, the commercial terms held: the company states all costs incurred through termination, including demobilisation, "will be reimbursed by the client," and no 2026 revenue had been booked on the suspended project. The exposure was managed even though it was lost.

**Guidance itself.** The refusal to quantify 2026 is the pressure point management is still not addressing. "In line with 2025" is a revenue statement. It says nothing about margin, nothing about cash, and nothing about the capital intensity that is currently consuming the profits.

The topic analysts are *not* pressing hard enough on is the one this dossier keeps returning to: the conversion of accounting profit into cash. Four analysts rate the stock a buy, none a sell, and the consensus target sits at €3.43 against a €2.16 share price. That is a street that has re-rated its price targets but not, visibly, its cash-flow model.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Free cash flow of −€557m in 2025**, the third consecutive annual decline, against record profit. The single most important number in this file.
🔴 **Cash down €770m; true net debt swung €893m to €623m** — in the year "net cash of €772m, beyond guidance" was the headline.
🔴 **Equity fell while earning record profit**; book value per share has not grown in five years. Returns are 3.1% on equity and 2.2% on capital — below any plausible cost of capital.
🔴 **2026 guidance withdrawn** (12 March 2026), by choice, at the moment of peak credibility.
🔴 **~€3.8bn of NEOM backlog terminated by the client** (March and 21 May 2026), against management's characterisation of the region as low-exposure.
🔴 **Effective tax rate of 49.6%** structurally caps what reaches shareholders.
🔴 **A corruption probe now touches the Messina bridge approval chain** (public June 2026): Rome prosecutors are investigating three individuals over alleged attempts to influence the Court of Auditors' review. Webuild and its Eurolink consortium are **not directly implicated**, but prosecutors are examining contacts with Eurolink and the Stretto di Messina company. This is headline risk on the single largest catalyst.

🟢 **The 2023–2025 plan was beaten decisively** — 19% compound revenue growth against a 10% target; EBITDA doubled from 2022.
🟢 **Margins genuinely expanded**, 7.2% → 8.6%, and the "gross margin contraction" the screener flags is a data-mapping artifact, not a real deterioration.
🟢 **NEOM terminations carry cost reimbursement** and no 2026 revenue was at risk — the contracts were written well.
🟢 **Backlog remains above €50bn** after the NEOM exit, with ~€3bn of new 2026 orders taken entirely in Italy, Australia and North America — a real and deliberate improvement in risk quality.
🟢 **Infrastructure demand is a secular tailwind**, not a melting base. Whatever ails this company, obsolescence is not it.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The terminology has moved in a specific direction: "Roadmap," "scale" and "growth" in the plan years; "de-risking," "low-risk markets," "discipline" and "margin and cash" in 2026. Note that last pair — management now names *cash* as a priority. That is the language of a team that knows exactly what this dossier's central table shows, and is telling you, in the only register available to it, that they intend to fix it.

The most revealing choice is the metric itself. A company reports the "net cash" definition that suits it — and Webuild's convention, which nets financial assets and receivables against borrowings, is common in European construction and defensible in an industry where cash sits in project vehicles. But the definitional gap is €1.4bn, and it is the difference between "net cash €772m" and "net debt €623m." Management did not hide the inputs. They chose the frame.

A second signal sits in the capital structure. Webuild is managed and coordinated by Salini Costruttori S.p.A. — a controlled company. That is not a red flag in itself, but it means the governance reset, activist campaign or strategic process that unlocks value in other special situations is largely unavailable here. There is no board to be flipped by an outside holder.

Third, and easy to miss: 2023's +€1.45bn of free cash flow was flattered by advances received on newly signed contracts — customers' money, arriving early. 2025's −€557m is that same cycle running in reverse as those projects execute. Across 2022–2025 cumulative free cash flow is roughly €940m, or ~€235m a year, against cumulative net profit of €568m. So the earnings *are* broadly backed by cash across a full cycle. The correct read is not "the profits are fake." It is "the profits are real, thin, violently lumpy, and worth far less than the EBITDA headline implies."

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING** — despite a record profit-and-loss statement, and I want to be precise about why, because the headline says the opposite.

Everything above the depreciation line improved in 2025. Everything below it got worse. Free cash flow fell for the third year running to −€557m, cash fell €770m, net debt swung €893m into deficit, and equity shrank while the company earned its best-ever profit. The 2023–2025 plan was beaten and then not replaced with another. The one region management had defended was terminated out from under them by its client. That combination — peak reported earnings, deteriorating cash, withdrawn guidance — is the trajectory, and it is deteriorating.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *EBITDA is not owner earnings here, and the gap is roughly four to one.* The entire "deep value" appearance of this stock rests on an enterprise value of €2.76bn against €1.16bn of EBITDA — 2.4 times, a fraction of where European peers trade. But that €1.16bn becomes €240m after depreciation, €410m of financial charges and a 49.6% tax rate, and it becomes *negative* after the €869m of capital spending the business actually requires. Value this company on EBITDA and it looks like a €4 stock. Value it on the ~€235–280m of normalised owner earnings it truly produces and it looks like a €2.50–2.80 stock, against €2.16 today. The discount is real but ordinary — roughly 8 to 9 times normalised earnings, not the 26% margin of safety the screener advertises. Any director sizing this on the EBITDA multiple is sizing on a number that has never reached a shareholder.

Two model artifacts to discard before they do damage: the input's "trailing twelve-month diluted EPS of €0.54" is wrong (audited 2025 diluted EPS is €0.24 on 984m shares — the €0.54 is a data error that would halve the apparent multiple), and "price/free cash flow 0.0x" is meaningless because free cash flow is negative. The screener's DCF fair value of €5.3 inherits these errors.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is a genuine regulatory-and-technical prequalification barrier combined with scale: the number of firms on earth that can bid a 3.3km suspension span, a major dam system or large-diameter tunnelling work is small, and that barrier is what wins a €50bn+ backlog and what let Webuild negotiate full cost reimbursement on a client-terminated contract. But the returns evidence refuses to call it wide: 2.2% return on capital and 3.1% return on equity are below any cost of capital, which is the market's way of saying the barrier keeps competitors out of the *bid* but not out of the *price*. **Moat trend: STABLE.** EBITDA margin expanded from 7.2% to 8.6% across the plan, and the deliberate rotation of new orders into Italy, Australia and North America should improve risk-adjusted margin quality further. Returns are improving from a poor base rather than eroding from a good one. This is not a widening moat, but it is not a melting one either.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** No structural force impairs the terminal value of building tunnels, dams, railways and bridges. Artificial intelligence does not displace it, digital channels do not disintermediate it, and the energy transition and infrastructure renewal cycles are, if anything, tailwinds. None of the controlled secular-decline themes applies to this name.

**So: fear-print or value trap?** Neither, cleanly — and a director should resist the pull to make it one or the other. This is not a structurally shrinking base, so it is not a value trap in the terminal sense; the demand is real and the backlog is real. But it is not a fear-print mispricing either, because the thing the market is discounting — that this company's accounting profits do not become cash, and that its capital intensity and tax rate keep returns below cost of capital — is *true*, and is corroborated by three consecutive years of deteriorating cash flow and five years of flat book value.
